rows.description: A teenager caught in a lie may add another to escape, or attack the person who found out. Shame is heavy, and the mind prefers escape to admission in the moment.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A parent or teacher caught in a small lie feels exposed. Admitting it simply and repairing teaches more about honesty than defending it.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult who admits the lie early, before being cornered, and takes the consequences, feels awful but lighter. Facing it keeps self-respect and often earns a second chance.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.description: A person caught in a lie states plainly what was false, why they said it, and what they will do differently, and accepts that trust may return slowly. Excuses and blaming the discoverer delay repair.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 18–22

rows.subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
rows.description: A parent, friend or partner who finds a lie can name what they know, ask why it felt necessary, and separate the person from the act. Traps and public shaming make hiding more likely.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 23–26

rows.subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
rows.description: A person weighs whether a lie was a small social smoothing, a pattern, or a serious betrayal with real cost. Response is proportionate, and repeated serious lies call for firm limits.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17

rows.subtopic: Catching someone else in a lie
rows.description: A person who discovers they were deceived for months feels shame and questions their judgement. Being fooled by someone practised at it is not a personal failing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17

rows.subtype: Telling the truth to a friend at a price [Actor]
rows.description: A teenager admits they broke something, or refuses to cheat with the group, and risks blame or being left out. The price is real, and the self-respect gained lasts longer.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young adult turns down a fake certificate, a bribe or a copied assignment, even when others succeed with it. They feel the fear of falling behind alongside the calm of a clean conscience.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26

rows.subtype: Admitting a mistake at work or college [Actor]
rows.description: A person reports their own error before it is found, and faces a scolding. The fear is strong, and the trust earned afterwards is greater than any protection silence would have given.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 13–17, 23–26
